title: Arcade Tile Run
story: An arcade has a floor game: a long strip of light-up tiles, each showing a score. Some scores are bonuses, like +4, and some are traps, like -5. You jump onto any tile you like, run forward across the tiles one by one, and jump off whenever you choose. Your score is the sum of every tile you touched.
You can see all the tiles before you start. If you pick the best place to jump on and off, what score do you get?
task: Write bestRun(tiles). Return the largest possible sum of a run of one or more consecutive tiles.
You must touch at least one tile, so if every tile is negative the answer is the least negative tile, not 0. Return only the score, not the positions.

examples.explanation: Jump on at the 4 and off after the 6: 4 - 1 + 6 = 9. Starting earlier at the 3 adds 3 - 5 = -2, which only hurts. Running on past the 6 hits the -8, and the 2 after it does not make up for it.
Every tile is a trap, but you must land on at least one. The best you can do is the single tile -2.

hints: Say you are standing on the 4 in [3, -5, 4, -1, 6, -8, 2] and want the best run that ends right here. Would you want to bring along the tiles before it, which add up to 3 - 5 = -2?

A run that ends at a tile either starts fresh at that tile, or extends the best run that ended at the tile before. Extend only if that earlier run has a positive total; a negative total only drags you down.
So for each tile: endingHere = max(tile, endingHere + tile). The answer is the largest endingHere you ever see, because the best run must end somewhere.

Walk once from left to right with two numbers: the best run ending at the current tile, and the best seen anywhere so far. Start both at the first tile (not 0), so an all-negative strip still gives the right answer.
bruteForce: Try every start and every end, and add up the tiles between them. With running sums that is about n²/2 runs to check.
For 100,000 tiles that is around 5 billion runs. The waste is that the run from 2 to 9 and the run from 3 to 9 share almost everything, yet each is treated as a brand-new question.

walkthrough: Ask a smaller question at every tile: what is the best run that ends exactly here? It is either this tile alone or this tile added to the best run ending one tile earlier. The overall answer is the biggest of these.
• 4: max(4, -2 + 4) = 4. Starting fresh wins, because the run behind us was negative.
Starting at the first tile rather than at 0 is what makes [-4, -2, -7] return -2. If you start best at 0 you are quietly allowing an empty run.
solution.timeWhy: One pass with two comparisons per tile.
solution.takeaway: For "best contiguous stretch" problems, track the best stretch ending at the current element. Extend it while it helps, restart when it has gone negative, and remember the best you have seen.
